opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, and I think it's one where there isn't a single right answer yet. It depends a lot on what you're trying to do.

Gaussian splats are fantastic as a representation for appearance. They give you really high-fidelity, photorealistic rendering, and they're fast. But fundamentally they're a bag of semi-transparent blobs. There's no notion of a surface, no notion of an object, no notion of mass or rigidity or anything you'd need for physics. So any time you want interaction, you have to bring that structure in from somewhere.

There are roughly a few families of approaches. One is the classical graphics route: you extract some kind of proxy geometry from the splats, like a mesh or a collision volume, segment the scene into objects, and then hand it to a traditional physics engine. The big advantage is that physics engines are mature, well understood, and stable. You get real-time rigid body simulation and decades of tooling. The downside is that the extraction step is lossy and brittle. Getting clean, watertight geometry out of splats is hard, segmentation is imperfect, and you need to guess physical properties like mass and friction that aren't in the captured data.

A second family simulates directly on the Gaussians themselves, treating them as particles in something like a material point method. That's elegant because the representation you render is the one you simulate, so deformation looks consistent. You can do soft bodies, cloth-like things, fluids. But it's expensive, it can be hard to control, and you still have to specify material parameters, which brings you back to the question of where that knowledge comes from.

The third direction, which I find most exciting long term, is more learned or generative. Instead of simulating physics explicitly, you rely on models that have absorbed priors about how the world behaves from huge amounts of data, like video models, and use them to predict plausible dynamics or to infer physical properties. That scales with data and can handle messy real-world stuff that's hard to hand-engineer. The tradeoff is controllability and consistency. A learned model might produce something that looks plausible but violates conservation laws, or isn't consistent over time, or can't be precisely controlled the way a game developer or roboticist needs.

So the tension is basically explicit structure versus learned priors. Explicit approaches give you control, precision, and guarantees but don't scale well to the diversity of the real world. Learned approaches scale and capture rich behavior but are harder to pin down. My guess is that the winning systems will be hybrids: an explicit 3D representation as the backbone, because that gives you persistence, consistency, and a way for people to interact with and edit the world, with learned components filling in what's hard to hand-specify, like segmentation, material properties, and plausible dynamics. Thinking in terms of persistent 3D worlds rather than just pixels is what makes that combination possible.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because splats are kind of a weird representation to do physics on. The thing that made Gaussian splatting take off is that it's this very unstructured, point-based thing. You've got millions of these little anisotropic blobs, each one is sitting wherever the optimization put it, there's no connectivity, no surface, no notion of what's inside versus outside an object. That's great for rendering, it's very fast, it looks beautiful. But the moment you want something to bounce or deform or get knocked over, all the stuff that physics engines have relied on for thirty years just isn't there.

So I'd say there are roughly three families of approaches, and they trade off along a couple axes.

The first is what I'd call "convert and go." You take the splats, you extract a mesh or some kind of proxy geometry, you hand that to an off-the-shelf engine, and then you bind the splats to that proxy. The splats are basically just a fancy texture riding on top of a skeleton. The upside is enormous, you get the entire mature physics stack for free: collisions, rigid bodies, cloth, joints, whatever. The downside is that mesh extraction from splats is still kind of lossy and fragile. Thin structures, foliage, fuzzy stuff, all the things splats are actually good at, those are exactly the things that mesh badly. And you end up with this gap between what the physics thinks the object is and what the viewer sees.

The second family is simulating directly on the Gaussians. Treat each Gaussian as a particle, or as a material point, and run something like MPM or a particle-based solver straight on them. PhysGaussian was the one that really got people's attention here. The appeal is you're not throwing away information, there's no proxy, the thing you simulate is the thing you render. And it handles the soft, squishy, continuum stuff really nicely. The cost is that you're now coupling your physics fidelity to your reconstruction quality in a way that can go wrong. Splats are placed to minimize photometric loss, not to be a good physical discretization. You get holes, you get interior regions that are just empty because the camera never saw them, and so you have to do things like fill in internal particles with heuristics. And it's slow compared to rigid-body engines, because you're paying for a continuum solver even when all you wanted was for a mug to fall off a table.

The third one, which I find most interesting from a research perspective, is learning the dynamics. Either you train a model to predict how the splats should move given some interaction, or you go further and use a video model as the physics prior and then fit the splats to what it hallucinates. This is the most general in principle, it can capture things that are really hard to simulate explicitly, like how a jacket crumples or how water looks. But you give up controllability and guarantees. There's no conservation of anything, objects can just drift through each other, and when it fails it fails in ways that are hard to debug because there's no parameter you can tweak.

The way I actually frame the tradeoff is: how much do you trust your reconstruction versus how much do you trust your prior? If you've got a dense, well-captured object and you need it to be physically faithful, go direct simulation. If you need interactivity at game framerates and a lot of objects, do the proxy thing and accept the visual mismatch. And if you're in the world of "I want it to look plausible and I don't care if it's physically correct," then learned dynamics are starting to be the right answer.

What I think is underexplored is the hybrid. Use a coarse proxy for collision and contact, which is the thing rigid-body engines are genuinely good at and learned models are bad at, and then use something learned or something continuum-based to handle the deformation and the appearance changes on top of that. The interface between those two layers is the hard part, but I think that's where a lot of the practical systems are going to end up, honestly.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: what do you want the representation to do? Gaussian splats give you a really nice representation for rendering, but that doesn’t automatically give you a representation for physics. If you want to push on an object, you need some notion of what belongs to that object, where its boundaries are, and how it should respond to forces. Those things aren’t necessarily determined by how it looks.

One approach is to separate those concerns. You have a mesh or some other underlying representation that handles simulation, and you attach the Gaussians to it for rendering. That lets you use existing physics machinery, which is attractive. The tradeoff is that now you have to construct that underlying representation and keep the appearance consistent with its motion. Something that looks great from the captured viewpoints might not hold up when you deform it or expose a surface you’ve never seen.

The other direction is to make the Gaussians more directly part of the simulation. That can be appealing for deformation, but you still have to define the material properties, the connections between elements, and how collisions work. A Gaussian that’s useful for reproducing an image isn’t necessarily the right unit of physical material.

So I wouldn’t expect one approach to win everywhere. For moving rigid objects around, a fairly simple collision model underneath a beautiful visual representation may be enough. For things that bend, tear, or interact in complicated ways, the choice of physical representation becomes much more important. And across all of these approaches, there’s a distinction between producing motion that looks plausible and recovering how the actual scene would behave. Images alone leave a lot of that ambiguous.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is, what do you want to do with the scene? Gaussian splats give you a really nice representation for rendering, but they don’t automatically tell you what’s solid, what’s connected, or how something should move when you push on it.

One approach is to keep the splats as the visual layer and build a separate representation for physics—maybe a mesh or a collection of simple collision shapes. Then you can use a conventional simulator and have the splats follow that geometry. That gives you a lot of control, but now you have to recover the geometry and keep those two representations consistent.

The other direction is to simulate the splats more directly, or attach them to particles in a deformable simulation. That can be attractive for things that bend or squish, but the primitives that make an image look good aren’t necessarily the right primitives for computing physical behavior. You still need assumptions about material properties, connectivity, and contact.

So I’d separate visual fidelity from physical fidelity. If you want an interactive experience that looks plausible, a fairly simple physics proxy might be enough. If you want to predict what would actually happen, then the hard part is identifying the underlying physical system. A beautiful reconstruction doesn’t, by itself, solve that problem.
